question: The direct reading magnetic compass is made aperiodic (dead beat) by:

options.text: using the lowest acceptable viscosity compass liquid.
keeping the magnetic assembly mass close to the compass point and by using damping wires.
using long magnets.
pendulous suspension of the magnetic assembly.

explanation: A dead-beat (aperiodic) compass settles without oscillating: magnet mass is concentrated near the pivot (small moment of inertia) and damping wires/liquid absorb the motion.

question: When turning right from 330° (C) to 040° (C) in the northern hemisphere, the reading of a direct reading magnetic compass will:

options.text: over-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will decrease the effect.
under-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will increase the effect.
under-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will decrease the effect.
over-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will increase the effect.

explanation: Turning through north (330→040) in the northern hemisphere the compass lags — it under-reads the turn — and liquid swirl adds to the error.

question: Coefficient A is corrected for:

options.text: using the compensation magnets.
moving the compass housing around its vertical axis.
removing disturbing magnetic material from the close vicinity of the compass.
de-gaussing (de-magnetising) the compass.

explanation: Coefficient A (constant deviation from compass/lubber-line misalignment) is removed by rotating the compass in its mounting.

question: A magnetic compass will be most effective at:

options.text: a position roughly half way between the magnetic poles.
the South Magnetic Pole.
the North Magnetic Pole.
the Equator.

explanation: The compass works on the horizontal component (H), which is strongest near the magnetic equator — roughly midway between the magnetic poles.

question: An aircraft has hard iron magnetism only, and this hard iron magnetism is represented by a red pole in relative bearing 070 from the compass. On what heading will the westerly deviation be maximum?

options.text: Heading 340.
Heading 200.
Heading 110.
Heading 020.

explanation: A red (north-seeking-type) pole repels the compass's north-seeking end. Deviation is maximum when that pole lies 90° to the magnetic meridian. With the pole at magnetic east (heading + 070 = 090 → heading 020°) the compass needle is pushed west → maximum westerly deviation.

question: The forces acting upon the compass needle in a stand-by compass in an aircraft, are:

options.text: the Earth’s magnetic field, the Coriolis effect and aircraft magnetism.
the total magnetic field in the compass location.
mechanic forces only.
the Earth’s magnetic field, the aircraft magnetic field and the effects of attitude and movement of the aircraft.

explanation: The needle is acted on by the Earth's field, the aircraft's own magnetism, and by forces due to aircraft attitude and acceleration (turning/acceleration errors).

question: An aircraft accelerates on a westerly heading in the northern hemisphere. The direct reading compass will:

options.text: indicate 270° .
indicate a turn to south.
indicate a turn to north.
indicate less than 270° .

explanation: Acceleration on east/west headings in the northern hemisphere shows an apparent turn towards north (ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South).

question: Which of the following will probably NOT result in a deviation change on a DRC?

options.text: A Walk-man headset placed close the compass.
Turning the ADF on in flight.
Relocating a steel iron construction in the cargo compartment close to the DRC.
Letting a passenger in cockpit the jump-seat put his mobile phone next to the DRC.

explanation: Radios such as the ADF are normally running during the compass swing, so switching them on should not change deviation; loose metal or electronics placed next to the compass will.

question: You are in the Northern hemisphere, heading 135 C on a Direct Reading Magnetic Compass. You turn right in a Rate 1 turn for 30 seconds. Do you roll out on an indicated heading of:

options.text: greater than 225.
less than 225.
equal to 225.
not possible to determine.

explanation: Turning through south in the northern hemisphere the compass leads (over-reads), so after a timed 90° turn the indicated heading is greater than 225°.

question: When an aircraft is moved to a place of lower magnetic latitude?

options.text: The deviation values will decrease because the horizontal component of the terrestrial field is becoming stronger.
Deviation values will change considerably and irregularly.
The deviation values will become more southerly.
The deviation values will increase.

explanation: Deviation from aircraft magnetism ∝ 1/H. At lower magnetic latitude H is stronger, so deviation decreases.

question: What is an advantage of a gyro-magnetic compass over a direct reading compass?

options.text: The gyro will always indicate the vertical.
There is a significant reduction in turning and acceleration errors.
Turning and acceleration errors are as large but more predictable.
There is a significant reduction in lag.

explanation: A gyro-magnetic (remote indicating) compass largely eliminates turning and acceleration errors.

question: The main reason for mounting the detector unit of a remote reading compass in the wingtip of an aeroplane is:

options.text: to ensure that the unit is in the most accessible position on the aircraft for ease of maintenance.
by having detector units on both wingtips, to cancel out the deviation effects caused by the aircraft structure.
to minimise the amount of deviation caused by aircraft magnetism and electrical circuits.
to maximise the units exposure to the earth's magnetic field.

explanation: The flux valve is put in the wingtip (or fin) to keep it away from aircraft magnetism and electrical fields, minimising deviation.

question: In discussing parameters P, Q and R of aircraft hard iron magnetism:

options.text: -Q indicates a blue pole in the left wing.
+P indicates a red pole in the aircraft nose.
+R indicates a red pole under the compass.
All 3 statements are correct.

explanation: Coefficient convention: +P = blue pole forward, +Q = blue pole in the right wing, +R = blue pole below the compass. So −Q means a blue pole in the left wing.

question: Concerning direct reading magnetic compasses, in the northern hemisphere, it can be said that:

options.text: on an Easterly heading, a longitudinal acceleration causes an apparent turn to the South.
on an Easterly heading, a longitudinal acceleration causes an apparent turn to the North.
on a Westerly heading, a longitudinal acceleration causes an apparent turn to the South.
on a Westerly heading, a longitudinal deceleration causes an apparent turn to the North.

explanation: Northern hemisphere: accelerate on E/W headings → apparent turn north; decelerate → apparent turn south (ANDS).

question: An aircraft is at 50° S 134° E heading 100° M. When the aircraft accelerates the direct reading compass will:

options.text: be deflected anticlockwise and indicate a turn to starboard.
be deflected anticlockwise and indicate a turn to port.
be deflected clockwise and indicate a turn to starboard.
be deflected clockwise and indicate a turn to port.

explanation: Southern hemisphere: acceleration on an easterly heading gives an apparent turn towards the south (here to starboard). For an indicated turn to starboard the magnet assembly rotates anticlockwise relative to the aircraft.

question: What is the purpose of the Annunciator in a gyromagnetic compass?

options.text: To indicate a mechanical failure within the compass.
To indicate an electrical failure within the compass.
To indicate when a compass swing should be carried out.
To achieve and indicate synchronisation of the gyro and the magnetic elements of the compass system.

explanation: The annunciator shows the synchronisation state between the gyro and the detector (flux valve) and helps achieve it.

question: When should a direct reading compass in an aircraft be swung?

options.text: After a large permanent change in magnetic latitude.
After being stored for a long period and frequently moved.
After a certain number of landings.
After a large permanent change in magnetic longitude.

explanation: A swing is needed after a large permanent change of magnetic latitude (the deviation values change with H).

question: You are turning from 330C to 040C in the Northern hemisphere, using timing. You stop the turn at the correct time. Before the direct indicating magnetic compass settles down, does it over-read or under- read, and does the effect of liquid swirl increase or decrease?

options.text: Under-read; increase.
Over-read; decrease.
Under-read; decrease.
Over-read; increase.

explanation: Turning through north in the northern hemisphere the compass under-reads, and liquid swirl increases the error.

question: An aircraft is heading 090° M at 45° S and accelerates. The needle of its direct reading compass will:

options.text: turn anticlockwise and indicate a turn to south.
turn clockwise and indicate a turn to north.
turn clockwise and indicate a turn to south.
turn anticlockwise and indicate a turn to north.

explanation: Southern hemisphere: accelerating on an easterly heading gives an apparent turn towards the south (heading increasing); the magnet turns anticlockwise relative to the aircraft.

question: Hard iron magnetism in aircraft may be caused by:

options.text: steel components, mainly in engines and undercarriage.
magnetic qualities of the cargo or baggage.
a strike of lightening.
All 3 answers are correct.

explanation: Permanent (hard-iron) magnetism comes from steel parts (engines, undercarriage), magnetised cargo carried in the aircraft and lightning strikes.

question: The sensitivity of a direct reading compass varies:

options.text: inversely with the vertical component of the earth’s magnetic.
directly with the horizontal component of the earth’s magnetic field.
directly with the vertical component of the earth’s magnetic field.
inversely with both vertical and horizontal components of the earth’s magnetic field.

explanation: Compass sensitivity (directive force) is proportional to H, the horizontal component.

question: In the calculation of deviation, the following headings are recorded: MH CH 358 356 091 087 182 186 273 271 Coefficient A is:
explanation: Deviation = MH − CH: +2, +4, −4, +2. Coefficient A = average = 4/4 = +1.

question: An aircrafts compass must be swung:

options.text: if the aircraft has been in the hangar for a long time and has been moved several times.
if the aircraft has been subjected to hammering.
every maintenance inspection.
after a change of theatre of operations at the same magnetic latitude.

explanation: Severe shocks (e.g. hammering, heavy landings, lightning) can alter the aircraft's permanent magnetism and require a compass swing.

question: At the magnetic equator, when accelerating after take off on heading West, a direct reading compass:

options.text: under reads the heading.
over reads the heading.
indicates the correct heading.
indicates a turn to the south.

explanation: At the magnetic equator Z = 0, so there is no acceleration error — the compass reads correctly.

question: An aircraft in the northern hemisphere is making an accurate rate one turn to the right. If the initial heading was 135° , after 30 seconds the direct reading magnetic compass should read:

options.text: less than 225°
more or less than 225° depending on the pendulous suspension used
more than 225°

explanation: Rate 1 for 30 s = 90° → 225°. Turning through south in the northern hemisphere the compass leads, so it reads more than 225°.

question: Permanent magnetism in aircraft arises chiefly from:

options.text: exposure to the earth’s magnetic field during normal operation.
hammering, and the effect of the earth’s magnetic field, whilst under construction.
the combined effect of aircraft electrical equipment and the earth’s magnetic field.
the effect of internal wiring and exposure to electrical storms.

explanation: Permanent (hard-iron) magnetism is acquired mainly during construction — hammering and riveting while lying in the Earth's field.

question: When accelerating on a westerly heading in the northern hemisphere, the compass card of a direct reading magnetic compass will turn:

options.text: clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the north
clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the south
anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the north
anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the south

explanation: Westerly heading, northern hemisphere, acceleration: apparent turn towards north, card turning anticlockwise (seen from above).

question: The purpose of compass check swing is to:

options.text: cancel out the horizontal component of the earth’s magnetic field.
cancel out the vertical component of the earth’s magnetic field.
measure the angle between Magnetic North and Compass North.
cancel out the effects of the magnetic fields found on board the aeroplane.

explanation: A check swing measures the remaining deviation (angle between magnetic and compass north) on several headings.

question: A direct reading compass is used at North Magnetic Latitude. Starting a right hand turn from heading 300 will result in:

options.text: at first a compass indication of a left hand turn.
the turn has to be broken off before the compass indicate the desired end heading 080.
the compass indication will lag during at least the first 90° of the turn.
All 3 answers are correct.

explanation: Turning through north at high northern magnetic latitude the compass may initially show the opposite turn, lags (under-reads) through north, so the turn must be stopped before the compass shows 080° — all three apply.

question: In the areas close to the magnetic poles compasses are not to any use in air navigation, mainly because:

options.text: The field strength of the Earth’s magnetic field is at it is weakest in this area.
The distance from the magnetic equator is too long.
The horizontal component of the Earth’s magnetic field is too weak.
The inclination is insufficient in these areas.

explanation: Near the magnetic poles H is too weak to give a directive force.

question: Deviation on MH 180 is -5 and on MH 000 it is +3. Calculate coefficient C:

options.text: Coefficient C = -1
Coefficient C = +4
Coefficient C = -2
Coefficient C = +8

explanation: Coefficient C = (dev on N − dev on S)/2 = (+3 − (−5))/2 = +4.

question: Hard iron magnetism in aircraft:

options.text: is permanent of nature.
will change with aircraft heading.
is easily compensated for by de-gaussing (de-magnetisation).
will be the same in all aircraft of the same type.

explanation: Hard-iron magnetism is permanent; it is independent of heading, and its deviation effect varies with heading.

question: Which one of the following is an advantage of a remote reading compass as compared with a standby compass?

options.text: It senses the magnetic meridian instead of seeking it, increasing compass sensitivity.
It is lighter than a direct reading compass because it employs, apart from the detector unit, existing aircraft equipment.
It eliminates the effect of turning and acceleration errors by pendulously suspending the detector unit.
It is more reliable because it is operated electrically and power is always available from sources within the aircraft.

explanation: The flux valve senses the direction of the magnetic meridian rather than physically seeking it, giving a stronger, steadier signal.

question: In direct reading magnetic compass, the effect of dip is counteracted by:

options.text: Low centre of gravity.
Compass liquid.
The shape of the casing.
Powerful magnets.

explanation: Dip is counteracted by pendulous suspension: the pivot is above the magnet's low centre of gravity.

question: The deviation will change with a change in aircraft heading:

options.text: Because the undesired magnetic pole then is moved relative to the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field.
Because the relative direction of the magnetic meridian is changed.
Because the strength of the undesired hard magnetism is changed.
Because the magnetic inclination will change whenever the heading is changed.

explanation: Turning the aircraft moves its magnetic poles relative to the Earth's field, so the deviating force changes with heading.

question: The directive force acting on a compass needle in an aircraft:

options.text: will always pull the north-seeking end down at southern magnetic latitudes and up at northern magnetic latitudes.
will be higher at high magnetic latitudes than near the magnetic equator.
is the resultant magnetic force in the horizontal plane in the position where the compass is installed.
will be cancelled by the compass compensation system

explanation: The directive force is the resultant horizontal magnetic force (Earth + aircraft) at the compass position.

question: A magnetic compass will show an apparent turn to the North in the Southern Hemisphere when:

options.text: the aircraft accelerates on 000 (C).
the aircraft accelerates on 090 (C).
the aircraft accelerates on 180 (C).
the aircraft decelerates on 270 (C).

explanation: Southern hemisphere: acceleration on E/W headings shows a turn towards south, deceleration towards north — so decelerating on 270° shows a turn north.

question: Soft iron magnetism in aircraft:

options.text: will not cause any compass deviation.
is non-permanent of nature, and cannot be reduced by de-gaussing (de-magnetisation).
is easily compensated for in the compass swing procedure.
will change at unknown times.

explanation: Soft-iron magnetism is induced (non-permanent), changing with heading and latitude; degaussing cannot remove it.

question: The type of compass least likely to suffer from parallax is:

options.text: direct reading compass.
remote reading compass.
directional indicator.
a standby compass.

explanation: A remote reading compass presents heading on a dial (no floating card behind a lubber line), so parallax is least.

question: A compass swing should be conducted:

options.text: with the radio equipment off.
with the engine shut down.
with no crew onboard
with the engine running.

explanation: The swing is done with engines running and electrical/radio equipment on, as in flight.

question: A Landing Compass:

options.text: Is used to establish aircraft magnetic heading during a compass swing.
Is painted on the ground at airfields to indicate the direction of the cardinal magnetic headings to observers on the ground or in the air.
Is the compass used as reference during landing.
Is a compass on which the runway direction for landing may be set. The variation information is printed on the map as isogonals.

explanation: A landing (datum) compass is set up on the ground to establish the aircraft's magnetic heading during a compass swing.

question: The directive force is:

options.text: H
Z
L
V

explanation: The directive force on a compass is H, the horizontal component.

question: With reference to the remote compass system. The precession rate of the gyro is kept low in order to:

options.text: maintain the gyro axis in the horizontal plane.
suppress turning and acceleration errors.
maintains the gyro axis in the vertical plane.
allow the master unit to follow the gyro unit.

explanation: The flux valve's precession of the gyro is kept slow so short-term turning/acceleration errors of the detector are averaged out.

question: In a typical remote reading compass, the gyro is kept aligned with the magnetic meridian by means of:

options.text: the Annunciator.
heading selector.
a torque motor
the gyro rigidity controller.

explanation: A torque (precession) motor slaves the gyro to the flux-valve signal.

question: In northern hemisphere, during an acceleration in an easterly direction, the magnetic compass will indicate:

options.text: a decrease in heading.
an increase in heading.
an apparent turn to the South.
a heading of East.

explanation: Northern hemisphere, easterly heading, acceleration → apparent turn north, i.e. a decrease in indicated heading.

question: Which of the following is an occasion for carrying out a compass swing on a Direct Reading Compass?

options.text: After an aircraft has passed through a severe electrical storm, or has been struck by lightning.
Before an aircraft goes on any flight that involves a large change of magnetic latitude.
After any of the aircraft radio equipment has been changed due to unserviceability.
Whenever an aircraft carries a large freight load regardless of its content.

explanation: A lightning strike or severe electrical storm can change the aircraft's permanent magnetism — swing required.

question: A direct reading compass is used. Accelerating an aircraft on heading 090 at South Magnetic Latitude will result in:

options.text: no change in compass indication.
a stable oscillation of the compass indication around heading 090.
an indication of a right turn on the compass.
an indication of a left turn on the compass.

explanation: Southern hemisphere: acceleration on 090° gives an apparent turn towards south — an indicated right turn.

question: Compass deviation is caused by:

options.text: The difference in the location of the Earth’s Magnetic and Geographic Poles.
The angle of magnetic dip.
The angle of inclination.
Aircraft magnetism distorting the Earth’s magnetic field.

explanation: Deviation is caused by the aircraft's own magnetism distorting the Earth's field at the compass.

question: Which of the following statements is correct concerning the effect of turning errors on a direct reading compass?

options.text: Turning errors are greatest on north/south headings, and are least at high latitudes.
Turning errors are greatest on east/west headings, and are least at high latitudes.
Turning errors are greatest on north/south headings, and are greatest at high latitudes.
Turning errors are greatest on east/west headings, and are greatest at high latitudes.

explanation: Turning errors are largest on north/south headings and increase with magnetic latitude.

question: Consider the following statements on coefficient A, as used to describe deviation:

options.text: coefficient A is the average deviation on all headings.
coefficient A will normally be calculated after coefficients B and C has been corrected for.
coefficient A may be calculated at any stage during a compass swing.
All 3 answers are correct.

explanation: Coefficient A is the mean deviation over the cardinal (and quadrantal) headings — constant on all headings.

question: The remote compass system remains synchronised in a turn because:

options.text: the follow up motor keeps the compass synchronised.
the precession circuit is activated causing the gyro to follow the turn.
it is sensing the earth’s electrical field automatically.
the signals from the detector unit to the signal Selsyn change at the same rate as the rotor of the signal Selsyn turns.

explanation: In a turn the detector signal and the signal selsyn rotor change together, so no error signal is generated and the system stays synchronised.

question: Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Turning errors are maximum when turning through north and south
Acceleration errors are maximum on east/west headings
Turning errors are maximum when turning through east and west
Acceleration errors are minimum on north/south headings

explanation: Turning errors are greatest through N and S and nil through E/W; acceleration errors are greatest on E/W and nil on N/S. So C is the false statement.

question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Turning through the nearer pole the compass is sluggish, so roll out late
Turning through the further pole the compass is sluggish, so roll out early
Turning through the further pole the compass is lively, so roll out early
Turning through the nearer pole the compass is sluggish, so roll out early

explanation: Through the nearer pole (north in the NH) the compass lags/under-reads, so you stop the turn before the compass reaches the desired heading (UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South).

question: When turning anticlockwise onto a southerly heading in the northern hemisphere, the turn should be stopped:

options.text: before the required heading is indicated
when the compass slows down
after the required heading is indicated
exactly when the required heading is indicated

explanation: Turning onto south in the NH the compass leads (over-reads), so it reaches 180° early — roll out after it passes the required heading (overshoot south).
